claim: Tuberculous meningitis has high mortality linked to excessive inflammation.
source: Tuberculous meningitis has high mortality, linked to excessive inflammation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established characteristic of TBM, drawing on general medical knowledge.

claim: Adjunctive anti-inflammatory corticosteroids reduce tuberculous meningitis mortality by only 30%.
source: However, adjunctive anti-inflammatory corticosteroids reduce mortality by only 30%, suggesting that inflammatory pathophysiology causes only a subset of deaths.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to prior studies in the introduction.

claim: In Vietnam, the survival benefit of anti-inflammatory corticosteroids was most pronounced in patients with a C/T promoter variant in the leukotriene A4 hydrolase (LTA4H) gene.
source: In Vietnam, the survival benefit of anti-inflammatory corticosteroids was most pronounced in patients with a C/T promoter variant in the leukotriene A4 hydrolase (LTA4H) gene encoding an enzyme that regulates inflammatory eicosanoids.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and refers to findings from prior Vietnam studies cited in the introduction.

claim: LTA4H TT patients with increased expression had increased survival, consistent with corticosteroids benefiting individuals with hyper-inflammatory responses.
source: LTA4H TT patients with increased expression had increased survival, consistent with corticosteroids benefiting individuals with hyper-inflammatory responses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data from the Vietnam cohort analysis.

claim: An Indonesia study did not find an LTA4H TT genotype survival benefit.
source: However, an Indonesia study did not find an LTA4H TT genotype survival benefit.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and refers to the Indonesia study cited in the manuscript.

claim: LTA4H TT genotype confers survival benefit that begins early and continues long-term in both Vietnam and Indonesia populations.
source: Here using Bayesian methods to analyse both studies, we find that LTA4H TT genotype confers survival benefit that begins early and continues long-term in both populations.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study based on Bayesian analysis of both cohorts.

claim: The LTA4H TT genotype survival benefit is nullified in the most severe cases with high early mortality.
source: This benefit is nullified in the most severe cases with high early mortality.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the Bayesian analysis.

claim: LTA4H genotyping together with disease severity assessment may target glucocorticoid therapy to patients most likely to benefit from it.
source: LTA4H genotyping together with disease severity assessment may target glucocorticoid therapy to patients most likely to benefit from it.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Tuberculous meningitis results in 20–25% mortality in HIV-negative individuals.
source: Despite effective antimicrobial therapy, it results in 20–25% mortality in HIV-negative individuals and ~40% mortality in HIV-positive individuals (Stadelman et al., 2020; Thwaites et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Tuberculous meningitis results in ~40% mortality in HIV-positive individuals.
source: Despite effective antimicrobial therapy, it results in 20–25% mortality in HIV-negative individuals and ~40% mortality in HIV-positive individuals (Stadelman et al., 2020; Thwaites et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A long-standing hypothesis suggests that an excessive intracerebral inflammatory response underlies TBM mortality.
source: A long-standing hypothesis that an excessive intracerebral inflammatory response underlies TBM mortality (Shane and Riley, 1953) led to multiple trials of adjunctive anti-inflammatory treatment with corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone) (Prasad et al., 2016; Wilkinson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Shane and Riley, 1953.

claim: A randomised controlled trial in Vietnam found that adjunctive dexamethasone improved survival by ~30%.
source: Findings from a randomised controlled trial (RCT) in Vietnam that adjunctive dexamethasone improved survival by ~30% led to it becoming standard of care treatment (Thwaites et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Thwaites et al., 2004.

claim: Adjunctive dexamethasone became standard of care treatment for TBM following the Vietnam RCT.
source: Findings from a randomised controlled trial (RCT) in Vietnam that adjunctive dexamethasone improved survival by ~30% led to it becoming standard of care treatment (Thwaites et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: The modest benefit of adjunctive dexamethasone treatment suggested a heterogeneity in glucocorticoid-responsiveness.
source: However, the modest benefit of adjunctive dexamethasone treatment suggested a heterogeneity in glucocorticoid-responsiveness (Donald and Schoeman, 2004; Schoeman and Donald, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Zebrafish model findings suggested that either deficiency or excess of leukotriene A4 hydrolase (LTA4H) increase susceptibility to TBM for opposite reasons - too little or too much inflammation.
source: The zebrafish findings suggested that either deficiency or excess of leukotriene A4 hydrolase (LTA4H), a key enzyme that regulates the balance of pro- and anti-inflammatory eicosanoids, increase susceptibility to TBM for opposite reasons - too little or too much inflammation (Tobin et al., 2012; Tobin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to zebrafish studies.

claim: A common human functional LTA4H promoter variant (rs17525495) comprises a C/T transition that controls LTA4H expression, with the T allele causing increased expression.
source: It became possible to test the prediction when a common human functional LTA4H promoter variant (rs17525495) was identified comprising a C/T transition that controlled LTA4H expression, with the T allele causing increased expression (Tobin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Tobin et al., 2012.

claim: A retrospective analysis of patient LTA4H rs17525495 genotypes in the Vietnam dexamethasone RCT cohort confirmed the prediction from zebrafish studies.
source: A retrospective analysis of patient LTA4H rs17525495 genotypes in the Vietnam dexamethasone RCT cohort confirmed the prediction (Thwaites et al., 2004; Tobin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Among HIV-negative patients in the Vietnam RCT, the survival benefit of dexamethasone was restricted to patients with the hyper-inflammatory TT genotype.
source: Among HIV-negative patients, the survival benefit of dexamethasone was restricted to patients with the hyper-inflammatory TT genotype, with CC patients potentially harmed by this treatment (Tobin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Tobin et al., 2012.

claim: CC patients were potentially harmed by dexamethasone treatment in the Vietnam RCT.
source: Among HIV-negative patients, the survival benefit of dexamethasone was restricted to patients with the hyper-inflammatory TT genotype, with CC patients potentially harmed by this treatment (Tobin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: Two new studies of the association of LTA4H genotype with TBM survival in HIV-negative patients were performed in Vietnam and Indonesia.
source: To further these findings, two new studies of the association of LTA4H genotype with TBM survival in HIV-negative patients were performed in Vietnam and Indonesia, respectively (Thuong et al., 2017; van Laarhoven et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: All patients in both the Vietnam and Indonesia studies received glucocorticoid adjunctive therapy because it had become standard of care.
source: Because glucocorticoid adjunctive therapy had become standard of care owing to the benefit observed in the randomised controlled trial (Thwaites et al., 2004), all patients received it in both studies.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: The Vietnam study confirmed the prediction that TT mortality is less than CC+CT mortality.
source: Therefore, the prediction that could be tested was that TT mortality is less than CC+CT mortality. Whereas the Vietnam study confirmed this prediction, the Indonesia study did not.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to the Vietnam study.

claim: The Indonesia study did not confirm the prediction that TT mortality is less than CC+CT mortality.
source: Therefore, the prediction that could be tested was that TT mortality is less than CC+CT mortality. Whereas the Vietnam study confirmed this prediction, the Indonesia study did not.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to the Indonesia study.

claim: The Vietnam cohort had an overall mortality of 18.8%.
source: The Vietnam cohort had an overall mortality of 18.8%, similar to that reported in the literature (Stadelman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and shown in Table 1.

claim: The Indonesia cohort had more than two-fold increased mortality in comparison with the Vietnam cohort.
source: A striking feature of the Indonesia cohort was its more than two-fold increased mortality in comparison with the Vietnam cohort.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Most of the Indonesia cohort deaths occurred early with a median time to death of eight days versus 50 days in Vietnam.
source: Moreover, most of the Indonesia cohort deaths occurred early with a median time to death of eight days versus 50 days in Vietnam (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The high early mortality in Indonesia raised the possibility that the impact of the LTA4H variant differs by disease severity.
source: This high early mortality raised the possibility that the impact of the LTA4H variant differs by disease severity, and may not be relevant in more severe disease (Fava and Schurr, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a hypothesis with citation.

claim: The effects of the LTA4H genotype were being masked by the preponderance of extremely severe cases in the Indonesia cohort.
source: If so, then the effects of the LTA4H genotype were being masked by the preponderance of extremely severe cases in the Indonesia cohort (Fava and Schurr, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a hypothesis with citation.

claim: The Vietnam cohort had a mean Glasgow Coma Score of 13.3 (range 3-15).
source: Glasgow Coma Score mean (range)	13.3 ** (3-15)
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The Vietnam cohort had significantly higher mean Glasgow Coma Score than the Indonesia cohort (Bayesian posterior probability > 0.99).
source: Glasgow Coma Score mean (range)	13.3 ** (3-15)	12.8 (5-15)
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with the ** notation indicating P > 0.99.

claim: In the Vietnam cohort, 163 patients (37.1%) were BMRC TBM grade 1, 206 (47.0%) were grade 2, and 70 (15.9%) were grade 3.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The Vietnam cohort had significantly more grade 1 patients than the Indonesia cohort (Bayesian posterior probability > 0.999).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with the *** notation indicating P > 0.999.

claim: The Indonesia cohort had significantly more grade 2 patients than the Vietnam cohort (Bayesian posterior probability > 0.999).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with the *** notation indicating P > 0.999.

claim: The Vietnam cohort had a median age of 41 years (range 18-93).
source: Age in years median (range)	41 *** (18-93)
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The Vietnam cohort was significantly older than the Indonesia cohort (Bayesian posterior probability > 0.999).
source: Age in years median (range)	41 *** (18-93)	28 (14-90)
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with the *** notation indicating P > 0.999.

claim: The Vietnam cohort had 83 deaths (18.8% overall mortality).
source: Overall mortality no. (%)	83 (18.8)
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The Indonesia cohort had significantly higher overall mortality than the Vietnam cohort (Bayesian posterior probability > 0.999).
source: Overall mortality no. (%)	83 (18.8)	146 (39.9) ***
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with the *** notation indicating P > 0.999.

claim: The Vietnam cohort had a median time to mortality of 50 days.
source: Time to median mortality (days)	50 ***
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The Vietnam cohort had significantly longer time to median mortality than the Indonesia cohort (Bayesian posterior probability > 0.999).
source: Time to median mortality (days)	50 ***	8
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 with the *** notation indicating P > 0.999.

claim: Cox regression modelling assumes that the ratio of hazard rates between groups is constant throughout the observed period.
source: Both studies used, as the primary metric of significance testing, Cox regression modelling, an approach that assumes that the ratio of hazard rates between groups is constant throughout the observed period (Bradburn et al., 2003; Greenland et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Cox regression could miss important differences in TBM studies because TBM can present acutely yet have a prolonged time-course with vastly differing mortality risks over time.
source: Therefore, this analytical method could miss important differences in these studies of TBM, a disease which can present acutely yet have a prolonged time-course with vastly differing mortality risks over time (Thuong et al., 2017; Thwaites et al., 2013; van Laarhoven et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of Cox regression with citations.

claim: Bayesian analysis is ideally suited to simultaneously estimate treatment effects in multiple subgroups.
source: Bayesian analysis is ideally suited to simultaneously estimate treatment effects in multiple subgroups because it results in different interactions with the number of results obtained which are much less problematic than those arising in frequentist analysis (Box 1 and Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a rationale for using Bayesian methods.

claim: Bayesian analysis enables the detection of significant differences that might be limited to just a part of the time-course.
source: Bayesian analysis also enables the detection of significant differences that might be limited to just a part of the time-course and therefore would allow analysis to be independent of the kinetics of death in the Vietnam and Indonesia cohorts.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of Bayesian methods.

claim: Bayesian paradigms understand probability in a real-world way, using it to indicate the plausibility of a particular conclusion.
source: Bayesian paradigms, unlike frequentist ones, understand probability in a real-world way, using it to indicate the plausibility of a particular conclusion (MacKay, 2003; Zampieri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Bayesian paradigms have less potential for bias arising from post-hoc analysis.
source: Finally, relevant to this re-analysis of completed clinical studies, Bayesian paradigms have less potential for bias arising from post-hoc analysis (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of Bayesian methods.

claim: The Indonesia cohort had more severe disease on presentation than the Vietnam cohort by both Glasgow Coma Score and modified British Medical Research Council TBM grade measures.
source: The Indonesia cohort had more severe disease on presentation by both measures (Table 1 and Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: 76% of Indonesia patients presented in Grade 2 versus 47% of the Vietnam patients.
source: Indeed, a detailed comparison of the Vietnam and Indonesia cohorts showed that 76% of Indonesia patients presented in Grade 2 versus 47% of the Vietnam patients (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The increase in Grade 2 patients in Indonesia was driven entirely by a shift from Grade 1 (9% vs 37% in Vietnam).
source: This increase was driven entirely by a shift from Grade 1 (9% vs 37% in Vietnam).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on data from Table 1.

claim: The Vietnam and Indonesia cohorts had nearly equal proportions of Grade 3 patients (15% each).
source: The cohorts had nearly equal proportions of Grade 3 patients (15% each).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on data from Table 1.

claim: The ~2 fold-increased overall mortality in Indonesia could be largely accounted for by a corresponding increase of Grade 2 patients (1.6 fold higher than Vietnam).
source: Therefore, the ~2 fold-increased overall mortality in Indonesia could be largely accounted for by a corresponding increase of Grade 2 patients (1.6 fold higher than Vietnam).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Disease severity as assessed by BMRC Grade or GCS at presentation is a strong predictor of earlier death.
source: Disease severity as assessed by BMRC Grade or GCS at presentation is also a strong predictor of earlier death (Fava and Schurr, 2017; Wang et al., 2019), and the Indonesia patients died sooner (median time to death 8 days versus 50 days in Vietnam) (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: In the original Vietnam study, the TT genotype was associated with survival and the CC and CT genotypes had similarly increased mortality over TT.
source: In the original Vietnam study, the TT genotype was associated with survival and the CC and CT genotypes had similarly increased mortality over TT (Thuong et al., 2017), so we compared TT survival to that of CT and CC combined (non-TT).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Thuong et al., 2017.

claim: The TT variant distribution did not differ by grade on presentation in the Vietnam cohort.
source: We first confirmed that the TT variant distribution did not differ by grade on presentation (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: In the overall Vietnam cohort, the TT genotype was associated with a survival advantage.
source: Bayesian analysis confirmed that the TT genotype was associated with a survival advantage in the overall cohort (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the overall Vietnam cohort, the TT survival advantage manifested early and persisted over most of the observation period.
source: Moreover, the analysis revealed that this survival advantage manifested early and persisted over most of the observation period (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the overall Vietnam cohort, TT survival was significantly higher than non-TT from day 39 onwards with maximum probability 0.98 and survival gap 11%.
source: In Vietnam, overall (A), TT survival was significantly higher than non-TT from day 39 onwards with maximum probability 0.98, survival gap 11%;
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In the overall Vietnam cohort, non-TT hazard rate was significantly higher than TT from day 4 to day 120, with their ratio peaking at 3 on day six and remaining >1 until day 223.
source: non-TT hazard rate was significantly higher than TT from day 4 to day 120, with their ratio peaking at 3 on day six and remaining >1 until day 223.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In Vietnam Grade 3 patients, TT survival was significantly higher from day 3 onwards with maximum probability 0.97 and survival gap 30%.
source: (D) Grade 3 TT survival was significantly higher from day 3 onwards with maximum probability 0.97, survival gap 30%.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In Vietnam Grade 3 patients, the TT hazard rate dropped from the start, while the non-TT hazard peaked at 16 times higher than TT on day 3.
source: The TT hazard rate dropped from the start, while the non-TT hazard peaked at 16 times higher than TT on day 3;
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In Vietnam Grade 3 patients, non-TT over TT hazard rate ratio remained >1 throughout the observation period.
source: non-TT over TT hazard rate ratio remained >1 throughout.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In the overall Indonesia cohort, TT survival was non-significantly higher than non-TT (maximum probability 0.92).
source: In Indonesia, overall (E), TT survival was non-significantly higher than non-TT (maximum probability 0.92);
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In the overall Indonesia cohort, the non-TT hazard rate was greater than the TT hazard rate from day 1 to day 13, significantly so (and by 2-fold) on days 2 and 3 (maximum probability 0.97).
source: the non-TT hazard rate was greater than the TT hazard rate from day 1 to day 13, significantly so (and by 2-fold) on days 2 and 3 (maximum probability 0.97).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In Indonesia Grade 2 patients, TT survival was significantly higher on days 4–32 with maximum probability 0.99 and survival gap 9%.
source: (G) Grade 2 TT survival was significantly higher on days 4–32 with maximum probability 0.99, survival gap 9%.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In Indonesia Grade 2 patients, the TT hazard rate dropped from the start, while the non-TT hazard peaked at five times higher than TT on day 3.
source: The TT hazard rate dropped from the start, while the non-TT hazard peaked at five times higher than TT on day 3.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In Indonesia Grade 2 patients, the non-TT over TT hazard rate ratio remained >1 until day 15.
source: The non-TT over TT hazard rate ratio remained >1 until day 15.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: The LTA4H TT association with survival was barely present in Vietnam Grade 1, a bit more in Grade 2, and strongest in Grade 3 where it reached significance.
source: When we stratified the Vietnam patients by grade and LTA4H genotype, we got a surprising result. The LTA4H TT association with survival was barely present in Grade 1, a bit more in Grade 2, and strongest in Grade 3 where it reached significance (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: In Vietnam, the bulk of the overall LTA4H TT association was being driven by Grade 3 patients who constituted only 15.9% of the cohort.
source: In fact, the bulk of the overall association was being driven by Grade 3 patients who constituted only 15.9% of the cohort (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: In Vietnam, non-TT patients were at greatest risk of dying within days of admission, a risk that diminished with time but remained greater than the TT patients throughout.
source: Non-TT patients were at greatest risk of dying within days of admission, a risk that diminished with time but remained greater than the TT patients throughout.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on hazard rate analysis.

claim: In Indonesia, the analysis of Grade 1 patients was uninformative as there was only one TT patient in this group who survived throughout.
source: For the grade-stratified cohorts, the analysis of Grade 1 patients was uninformative as there was only one TT patient in this group who survived throughout (Table 2 and Figure 2F; also see Appendix 2, section 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Table 2 and Figure 2F.

claim: In Indonesia Grade 2, the TT survival effect was significant, in contrast to Grade 2 Vietnam.
source: In Grade 2, the TT survival effect was significant, in contrast to Grade 2 Vietnam (compare Figure 2G–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: In Indonesia Grade 3, the LTA4H TT effect was absent.
source: In Grade 3, the LTA4H TT effect was again absent (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2H.

claim: In both Vietnam and Indonesia, survival of CC and CT patients was not significantly different at any time during the analysis for the overall cohort and for each of the three grades.
source: As in Vietnam, survival of CC and CT patients was not significantly different at any time during the analysis for the overall cohort and for each of the three grades (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The LTA4H TT benefit was weaker and less prolonged in Indonesia Grade 2 than in Vietnam Grade 3.
source: We saw that the LTA4H TT benefit was weaker and less prolonged in Indonesia Grade 2 than in Vietnam Grade 3 (compare Figure 2G to D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Non-TT patients had similar mortality in Indonesia Grade 2 and Vietnam Grade 3.
source: Non-TT patients had similar mortality in Indonesia Grade 2 and Vietnam Grade 3 (compare Figure 2G to D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Within each cohort, mortality risk increased with grade severity.
source: We confirmed by Bayesian analysis that within each cohort, mortality risk increased with grade severity (Thuong et al., 2017; van Laarhoven et al., 2017; Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations and reference to Figure 3.

claim: In both cohorts, from early on, Grade 1 survival was significantly greater than Grade 2, which was significantly greater than Grade 3.
source: From early on, Grade 1 survival was significantly greater than Grade 2, which was significantly greater than Grade 3 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The risk of increased mortality with higher grade was highest early but was sustained long-term.
source: The hazard rate ratios highlighted that while the risk of increased mortality with higher grade was highest early, it was sustained long-term (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 3.

claim: There was an increased grade-for-grade risk of mortality in Indonesia over Vietnam.
source: Importantly, both the survival and hazard rate analyses again pointed to an increased grade-for-grade risk of mortality in Indonesia over Vietnam.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of Figure 3.

claim: Vietnam survival probability was higher in all grades, and significantly so for Grades 2 and 3 with survival gaps of 18% and 24%, respectively.
source: Vietnam survival probability was higher in all grades, and significantly so for Grades 2 and 3 with survival gaps of 18% and 24%, respectively (Figure 4A,C and E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Hazard rates did not differ significantly between the cohorts in Grade 1.
source: Similarly, hazard rates did not differ significantly between the cohorts in Grade 1 (Figure 4B), but there was a significant and substantial increase in early hazard rates for Indonesia Grades 2 and 3 (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4.

claim: There was a significant and substantial increase in early hazard rates for Indonesia Grades 2 and 3 compared to Vietnam.
source: Similarly, hazard rates did not differ significantly between the cohorts in Grade 1 (Figure 4B), but there was a significant and substantial increase in early hazard rates for Indonesia Grades 2 and 3 (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The increased mortality in Indonesia was not because the Indonesia patients had more severe disease within each grade as reflected in the GCS.
source: We ruled out the possibility that this increased mortality was because the Indonesia patients had more severe disease within each grade as reflected in the GCS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of GCS data.

claim: Indonesia patients had somewhat more severe disease in Grade 2, but in Grade 3 where the difference was the most pronounced, they had milder disease.
source: While they had somewhat more severe disease in Grade 2, in Grade 3 where the difference was the most pronounced, they had milder disease (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The inherent higher mortality associated with more severe disease on presentation was sharply accentuated in Indonesia.
source: In sum, these analyses show that the inherent higher mortality associated with more severe disease on presentation was sharply accentuated in Indonesia.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Indonesia grade 2 patients experienced similar mortality risk as Vietnam Grade 3 patients.
source: Indonesia grade 2 patients experienced similar mortality risk as Vietnam Grade 3 patients with the Indonesia Grade 3 patients experiencing far greater mortality.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Indonesia Grade 3 patients experienced far greater mortality than Vietnam Grade 3 patients.
source: Indonesia grade 2 patients experienced similar mortality risk as Vietnam Grade 3 patients with the Indonesia Grade 3 patients experiencing far greater mortality.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the findings.

claim: The higher mortality in Indonesia could potentially explain the finding that the LTA4H TT survival advantage did not extend to Indonesia Grade 3 patients.
source: This higher mortality could potentially explain the finding that the LTA4H TT survival advantage did not extend to Indonesia Grade 3 patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference.

claim: The TT genotype advantage, in response to corticosteroid treatment, may be overridden by other factors that cause extreme mortality.
source: It may be that the TT genotype advantage, in response to corticosteroid treatment, is overridden by other factors that cause extreme mortality.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculative conclusion.

claim: The beneficial effect of fluoroquinolones in TBM is present in Grade 1 or 2 disease, but lost in Grade 3 disease.
source: The beneficial effect of fluoroquinolones in TBM is present in Grade1 or 2 disease, but lost in Grade 3 disease (Thwaites et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation.

claim: Grade 2 Indonesia overall mortality risk was virtually identical to Grade 3 Vietnam (38% versus 37.9%).
source: Tellingly, Grade 2 Indonesia overall mortality risk was virtually identical to Grade 3 Vietnam (38% versus 37.9%), suggesting that this level of overall mortality represents the boundary of the beneficial effect of LTA4H TT.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on data from Table 1.

claim: A mortality level of about 40% represents the boundary of the beneficial effect of LTA4H TT.
source: Tellingly, Grade 2 Indonesia overall mortality risk was virtually identical to Grade 3 Vietnam (38% versus 37.9%), suggesting that this level of overall mortality represents the boundary of the beneficial effect of LTA4H TT.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data.

claim: LTA4H TT efficacy was limited by other factors that cause mortality independent of severity grade on presentation.
source: Thus, LTA4H TT efficacy was limited by other factors that cause mortality. These factors appear independent of severity grade on presentation, and if they exceed a threshold (represented by about ~40% mortality) then the beneficial effect of LTA4H TT is lost.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the findings.

claim: If LTA4H genotype-independent mortality factors exceed a threshold (represented by about ~40% mortality) then the beneficial effect of LTA4H TT is lost.
source: These factors appear independent of severity grade on presentation, and if they exceed a threshold (represented by about ~40% mortality) then the beneficial effect of LTA4H TT is lost.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the findings.

claim: The patient populations, hospital care protocols and the availability of intensive care differed between each study site.
source: A limitation of this study is that we cannot definitively determine the causes of this LTA4H genotype-independent excess Grade 3 mortality in Indonesia because the patient populations, hospital care protocols and the availability of intensive care differed between each study site.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation.

claim: Better ancillary care was possible in Vietnam where all patients were enrolled into a clinical trial versus only 17% in Indonesia.
source: One possibility is that better ancillary care was possible in Vietnam where all patients were enrolled into a clinical trial versus only 17% in Indonesia (Thuong et al., 2017; van Laarhoven et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claim: The excess Grade 3 Indonesia mortality peaked within days.
source: The excess Grade 3 Indonesia mortality peaked within days, and optimized respiratory support, in particular, would be essential to keep patients alive through the early high risk stage in order allow for anti-inflammatory effects of corticosteroids to benefit the TT patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the data analysis.

claim: Optimized respiratory support would be essential to keep patients alive through the early high risk stage to allow for anti-inflammatory effects of corticosteroids to benefit the TT patients.
source: The excess Grade 3 Indonesia mortality peaked within days, and optimized respiratory support, in particular, would be essential to keep patients alive through the early high risk stage in order allow for anti-inflammatory effects of corticosteroids to benefit the TT patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation.

claim: The beneficial effect of dexamethasone to the LTA4H TT group may not have had time to come into play in Grade 3 Indonesia patients.
source: Thus the beneficial effect of dexamethasone to the LTA4H TT group may simply not have had time to come into play in Grade 3 Indonesia patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation.

claim: Indonesia Grade 3 patients may have presented with a greater degree of dysregulated inflammation in a manner not revealed by standard metrics of judging disease severity.
source: A second possibility is that Indonesia Grade 3 patients presented with a greater degree of dysregulated inflammation in a manner not revealed by standard metrics of judging disease severity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation.

claim: If Indonesia Grade 3 patients had greater dysregulated inflammation, then corticosteroids might no longer be beneficial.
source: If this were the case then corticosteroids might no longer be beneficial.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation.

claim: Both TT and non-TT patients in Indonesia Grade 3 suffered identical excess mortality risk.
source: Since both TT and non-TT patients suffered identical excess mortality risk, its cause would have been LTA4H-independent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the data.

claim: Indonesia patients tended to be younger than Vietnam patients in all grades.
source: Indonesia patients tended to be younger than Vietnam patients in all grades (Table 1), and perhaps were more prone to develop such a response.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Table 1.

claim: Younger Indonesia patients may have been more prone to develop dysregulated inflammation.
